name: Paul’s Missionary Journeys and Strategy
path: New Testament Studies: Life and Doctrine in Christ
Acts and the Founding of the Church

objectives.text: Identify Paul as a man God sent to travel to many places to tell people about Jesus
Name Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, and Luke as helpers who traveled with Paul
Retell the story of Paul's shipwreck and how God kept everyone on the ship alive as He had promised
Retell how Paul and Silas prayed and sang in the Philippian jail and how the jailer and his household came to believe
Trace on a map the cities Paul and Barnabas visited on the first missionary journey
Describe Paul's pattern of preaching first in the synagogue and then turning to the Gentiles
Explain how Paul and Barnabas responded when the crowd at Lystra tried to worship them as gods
Explain why Paul often stayed and preached in large cities such as Corinth and Ephesus
Describe how Paul worked as a tentmaker to support himself so he would not burden the churches
Compare how the Jews of Berea and Thessalonica responded to Paul's preaching, including the Bereans' daily examination of the Scriptures
Explain how the Holy Spirit called Paul and Barnabas and how the church at Antioch sent them out with prayer and fasting
Explain how the Spirit closed doors in Asia and Bithynia and how the Macedonian vision directed Paul into Europe
Describe how Paul returned to strengthen new churches and appointed elders to lead them
Construct a map of Paul's three missionary journeys and his voyage to Rome with key events labeled
Analyze how Paul's Areopagus speech moves from creation and the Athenians' own altar and poets to the call to repent and the resurrection
Analyze how the riot at Ephesus shows the gospel confronting idolatry and the trade built around it
Connect the founding of churches in Acts to the letters Paul later wrote to those same churches
Explain how Paul used his Roman citizenship and appeals to Roman law to protect the mission and bring the gospel before rulers
Analyze Paul's farewell address to the Ephesian elders as a summary of his ministry aims and methods
Analyze how Luke's account of Paul's journeys shows the gospel advancing from Jerusalem to Rome as Jesus foretold
Explain how the Reformed tradition relates God's sovereign election to Paul's urgent preaching, using texts where God's choosing and the preaching of the gospel appear together
Evaluate how Paul adapted his approach for Jewish and Gentile audiences while keeping the message of the cross and resurrection unchanged
Evaluate which features of Paul's strategy, such as urban centers, teams, and local elders, can guide missions today, distinguishing what Acts describes from what it commands
Develop a written theological account of suffering in Christian mission drawn from Paul's hardships and his own explanation of them

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (boat travel became Paul's calling to travel, helpers, shipwreck, map tracing, synagogue pattern, big cities, Berea vs Thessalonica, Macedonian call, Areopagus, Ephesus riot, churches and letters, Spirit's direction, map construction, contextualization, urban strategy, suffering). Moved the Spirit's role earlier and split it into the Antioch sending and the Macedonian redirection, moved the three-journey map from grade 10 to 6, and reframed the strategy defense as evaluating descriptive vs prescriptive application. Recast the cost of discipleship objective as a written theological account so it rests on what students know rather than personal experience. Added Philippian jail, Lystra, tentmaking, appointing elders, Roman citizenship, Miletus farewell, Acts 1:8 trajectory, and election and missions with Reformed confessional anchors. Gave every objective verse-level references, replacing the whole-section citation of Acts 13-14 with precise ranges, and avoided Pentecost, Jerusalem church, and Council material left to sibling sub-topics.
